definition: Suffrage means the right to vote in political elections.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word suffrage. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know suffrage should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The museum's centennial exhibit on suffrage displayed the sashes, the petitions, and the first ballot marked by a woman in the county.
Petition is far weaker than suffrage: petitioners may ask and hope while others decide, but suffrage puts the decision itself into the citizen's hands, one ballot at a time.
Sovereignty goes far beyond suffrage: suffrage gives each citizen a share in choosing who governs, while sovereignty is the supreme authority itself — the final power that answers to no one above it.

Suffragium built almost nothing else in English — suffragist and suffragette are its only working descendants, both coined during the long campaign for the vote, and both still carrying the original meaning on their sleeves.
Suffrage means the right to vote in political elections.
For decades the mill town's charter tied suffrage to property, so a foreman who rented rooms above the mill could be taxed for the new bridge but never vote on it; the charter finally fell in 1911.

Suffrage is the right itself — narrower than citizenship, which that foreman held all along, and more concrete than 'political voice.' When histories speak of universal suffrage, they mean one measurable thing: every adult may cast a ballot that counts.
Suffrage is precise and a little marble-columned: universal suffrage, women's suffrage, the suffrage movement.
It names the right, never the act or the paper — you exercise suffrage by casting a ballot, and the ballot is what you drop in the box.
And despite the sound, it shares nothing with suffering; a sentence about hardship wants a different word entirely.

In 1869, a thinly settled western territory did something no state had dared: it granted full suffrage to women.
The legislators' motives were mixed -- some believed in the principle, others simply hoped headlines would draw new settlers.
Whatever the reasons, the right itself was real: women registered, and that September they cast ballots alongside men.
When the territory later applied for statehood, congressmen demanded it abandon the experiment.
The territory's answer went back by telegram: it would stay out of the union a hundred years rather than surrender the right its women already held.
